corrected_claim.title: S&P (2011) and Fitch (2023) U.S. downgrades predate Trump’s second term
corrected_claim.description_short: S&P downgraded U.S. credit in 2011 and Fitch in 2023, before Trump’s second term.
corrected_claim.description_medium: Standard & Poor’s lowered the U.S. long-term sovereign rating from AAA to AA+ on August 5, 2011. Fitch lowered it from AAA to AA+ on August 1, 2023, citing fiscal deterioration, debt-ceiling brinkmanship, and governance concerns. Both decisions predated Trump’s second term and cannot support the original attribution to policies adopted in 2025.
corrected_claim.description_long: Standard & Poor’s lowered the United States’ long-term sovereign credit rating from AAA to AA+ on August 5, 2011. Its rating-action report cited fiscal risks and concerns about policymaking and governance. Fitch made a separate downgrade from AAA to AA+ on August 1, 2023. Reuters reported Fitch’s stated reasons, including expected fiscal deterioration, repeated debt-ceiling negotiations, and a perceived decline in governance. These were two distinct rating decisions taken years apart. Both occurred before Donald Trump’s second term, so neither can be attributed to policies adopted in 2025. The cited sources support the dates, rating changes, and agency rationales described here. They do not establish that Trump’s policies caused either decision, or that these actions alone raised annual debt-service costs by billions of dollars. The frozen entry also refers to all three major rating agencies by 2025, but the two cited documents do not establish that broader claim. This correction retains the historical downgrades while removing unsupported causal and financial-effect assertions.

exact_gap: The sources support the dates and agency rationales for the S&P and Fitch downgrades but not the original Trump-policy causal attribution or quantified debt-service effect.
access_notes: The S&P rating-action report and Reuters account of Fitch were directly retrieved; both URLs support the mapped rating action and stated rationale.

corrected_claim.title: Saudi Arabia announces a $600 billion U.S. investment commitment during Trump’s Gulf visit
corrected_claim.description_short: Saudi Arabia announced a $600 billion U.S. investment commitment during Trump’s May 2025 Gulf visit.
corrected_claim.description_medium: During Trump’s May 2025 Gulf visit, Saudi Arabia announced a $600 billion commitment to invest in the United States. Reuters later compared the White House’s larger headline total with its own tally of specified deals and reported that many corporate agreements were nonbinding memorandums. The announcements do not establish completed investment or an exchange for favorable treatment of Trump-linked businesses.
corrected_claim.description_long: During President Donald Trump’s May 2025 Gulf visit, Saudi Arabia announced a $600 billion commitment to invest in the United States, Reuters reported on May 13. Reuters’ May 16 review examined the larger White House total for combined Gulf deals. It said the White House cited more than $2 trillion, while Reuters’ tally of specifically announced deals exceeded $700 billion; the report also said many corporate agreements were nonbinding memorandums of understanding. These sources support describing a Saudi investment commitment and the uncertainty around headline totals. A commitment announcement is not proof that the full amount was invested, and the Reuters analysis distinguishes broad announcements from identifiable deals. The material does not show that Gulf governments were pressured to invest in Trump-linked entities or that an investment commitment was exchanged for favorable U.S. treatment. Nor does the amount describe money paid to a Trump-family business. The corrected entry is limited to the public announcement and Reuters’ analysis of deal totals. Claims about a bargain, completed transfers, or direct private benefit require evidence about a specific agreement and subsequent transaction.

exact_gap: The Reuters reports document announcements and deal-status uncertainty, not pressure, quid pro quo, completed investment of the headline amounts, or direct Trump-family benefit.
access_notes: Both Reuters reports were retrieved; the May 13 report supports the Saudi commitment and the May 16 analysis supports the deal-total qualifications.

corrected_claim.description_long: On January 24, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a memorandum reinstating the 2017 Mexico City Policy and revoking a 2021 presidential memorandum on the subject. The document directs the Secretary of State, in coordination with the Secretary of Health and Human Services and to the extent allowable by law, to implement a plan extending the reinstated policy’s requirements to global-health assistance furnished by all federal departments and agencies. The distinction between reinstatement, planning, and later implementation matters: the memorandum is a directive, not a record of every grant decision or service change that followed. Its text does not say that all U.S. aid ended for every organization that mentioned abortion, nor does it quantify changes in family-planning, HIV, or maternal-health funding or outcomes. The corrected title and descriptions retain the supported executive action and date while narrowing the original claim about an immediately effective, dramatically expanded funding cutoff. Any claim about a named recipient, a canceled award, or health effects requires specific implementation or program evidence beyond this memorandum.

corrected_claim.title: EO 14173 revises federal contracting and grant terms on unlawful DEI programs
corrected_claim.description_short: EO 14173 revoked EO 11246 and directed new contract and grant terms addressing DEI programs that violate federal anti-discrimination law.
corrected_claim.description_medium: Signed January 21, 2025, Executive Order 14173 revoked EO 11246 and directed agencies to include terms in federal contracts and grants requiring compliance with applicable anti-discrimination laws and certification that recipients do not operate DEI programs that violate those laws. It did not categorically ban all DEI activity at every institution receiving federal funds.
corrected_claim.description_long: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14173, “Ending Illegal Discrimination and Restoring Merit-Based Opportunity,” on January 21, 2025. The order revoked Executive Order 11246, which had set affirmative-action requirements for federal contractors. It also directed agency heads to include terms in federal contracts and grant awards requiring recipients to comply with applicable federal anti-discrimination laws and to certify that they do not operate DEI programs that violate those laws. The text thus addresses specified contracting and grant conditions and unlawful programs as defined by the order; it does not establish a categorical ban on every DEI activity at every university, hospital, nonprofit, or other institution receiving any federal money. The Federal Register text also sets agency implementation directions, but the order alone does not show how every agency applied them, whether a specific recipient lost funding, or how courts later interpreted its scope. The corrected account replaces the frozen entry’s universal-ban claim with the order’s stated actions and date. Claims about an individual institution, grant termination, or injunction require separate records.

exact_gap: The order does not state a universal ban; the scope and outcomes for particular recipients depend on agency terms and legal proceedings.
access_notes: The Federal Register text was retrieved and supports the order’s date, revocation, and contract/grant provisions.

corrected_claim.title: Members of Congress file impeachment resolutions against judges after adverse rulings
corrected_claim.description_short: Roll Call reported four impeachment resolutions against three judges after rulings that paused or slowed Trump administration actions.
corrected_claim.description_medium: Roll Call reported that by March 11, 2025, members of Congress had filed four impeachment resolutions against three federal judges following rulings that temporarily paused or slowed Trump administration actions. The article also reported judges’ concerns about using impeachment in response to decisions. It does not document threats of IRS audits or DOJ investigations by Trump officials.
corrected_claim.description_long: Roll Call reported on March 11, 2025, that members of Congress had filed four impeachment resolutions against three federal judges after decisions temporarily pausing or slowing Trump administration actions. The article describes resolutions filed by Representatives Andy Ogles, Derrick Van Orden, and Eli Crane against Judges Amir Ali, John Bates, and Paul Engelmayer. It also quotes federal appellate judges warning that impeachment should not be used to short-circuit the appellate process when lawmakers disagree with a judicial decision. These are congressional actions and judicial responses documented in the report. The article does not establish that President Trump or senior officials threatened IRS audits or Justice Department investigations against judges, nor that the White House directed the resolutions. It also does not show that a judge was removed or that the resolutions changed the underlying cases. The corrected record therefore focuses on the verifiable impeachment activity and leaves the original retaliation allegation unsupported by this source. A claim about an executive threat would need direct evidence such as a documented statement, directive, or investigation record.

exact_gap: The source documents congressional resolutions and judicial responses, not executive investigative threats or White House direction.
access_notes: Roll Call’s March 11 report was retrieved; it supports the resolution count, timing, named filings, and judges’ responses.
